opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to happen gradually, and probably less dramatically than people imagine. The first thing to notice is that management is a bundle of tasks. A lot of it is information processing: keeping track of what people are working on, synthesizing reports, figuring out where the bottlenecks are, allocating resources, and giving feedback. Some of those pieces are already within reach of current systems, so I'd expect AI to start out as an assistant to human managers rather than a replacement. It'll draft the performance review, summarize the state of a project, flag that some team is falling behind, and the human manager will make the final call.

Over time, as the systems get more reliable and as they're able to operate over longer horizons with more context, you'd see the share of the decision-making that's effectively delegated to the AI go up. At some point the human is mostly rubber-stamping, and then the question becomes whether you need the human there at all. I think the recognition happens through competition more than through anyone sitting down and deciding AI managers are good now. Some firms will lean into it earlier, maybe smaller firms or startups that have less organizational inertia, and if they outperform, others will be pressured to follow. That's how most general-purpose technologies have diffused historically. It's not that people are convinced by argument, it's that the firms that adopt them do better and either grow or get imitated.

There are some frictions specific to management, though. Management involves a lot of trust and accountability. People want someone to be responsible when things go wrong, and there are legal and cultural norms around who gets to hire and fire, who signs off on things. Those norms will slow adoption somewhat, and you might see a period where there's a nominal human in charge for liability reasons even when the AI is doing most of the substantive work. Workers may also resist being managed by an AI, at least initially, though I suspect that resistance fades faster than people expect if the AI turns out to be fairer or more responsive than a typical human boss.

So my overall picture is that it comes in through the back door: first as a tool, then as the thing actually doing the job with a human nominally on top, and eventually as the obvious default once the performance gap is large enough that it's hard to justify doing it any other way. And I'd expect management to be one of the later things to be fully automated rather than one of the first, because it depends on long-horizon planning, coordinating many agents, and handling messy, open-ended situations. Those are exactly the capabilities current systems are weakest at.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradual adoption and competition-driven diffusion, but does not clearly say recognition will lag significantly behind the capabilities’ emergence.

r002.rationale: It predicts AI will first assist human managers with tasks such as drafting reviews, summarizing projects, and flagging bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's going to happen more slowly and more unevenly than people expect, and the reason is that management is a capability you mostly can't demonstrate on a benchmark.

If you look at how capabilities have been recognized so far, there's usually some fairly legible signal. Coding has tests you can run, math has answers you can check, and so when a model gets good at those things, people notice within months. Management is different. The thing you're evaluating is whether a system can take a vague objective, decompose it into tasks, allocate them across people or other agents, monitor progress, notice when something is going wrong, and change the plan. The feedback on whether you did that well arrives weeks or months later, and it's confounded by everything else going on in the organization. So even if models become quite good at this, it's hard for anyone to prove it in a way that would convince a skeptic.

My expectation is that it gets recognized bottom-up rather than top-down. The first place you'll see it is inside AI systems themselves, where you have one model orchestrating many agents on a long software task. That's a management problem, it's just that the subordinates happen to be other copies of the model. Those setups generate a lot of data on what works, and the labs will iterate on it because it directly affects the products they ship. Then you'll see it leak into small firms and startups, because they have the least institutional resistance and the most to gain. A five-person company that effectively has an AI project manager coordinating a hundred agents can do things that previously required a much larger organization, and that's the kind of thing that becomes visible through outcomes rather than through anyone being persuaded in advance.

Large organizations will be last, and I think they'll be last for reasons that aren't really about capability. Management roles are tied up with status, accountability, and legal responsibility. Someone has to be the person who gets fired when things go wrong, and it's not obvious a company wants that to be a model. So adoption there will look less like "we replaced the managers" and more like managers increasingly delegating the mechanical parts of their job, until at some point the human in the loop is mostly there for accountability rather than for decision-making.

The other thing I'd say is that I think people underestimate how much of the bottleneck here is not the models but the surrounding infrastructure. For a system to manage effectively, it needs persistent context, it needs to be able to take actions in the environment, it needs access to the same information a human manager would have. A lot of that doesn't exist yet in a form that's easy to plug a model into. So even if the raw capability shows up, the diffusion lags, and I'd guess that lag is measured in years rather than months. That's consistent with how most general-purpose technologies have gone, and I don't see a strong reason to think this one is different, at least until you get to the point where AI systems are building that infrastructure for themselves.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects recognition to happen more slowly than people expect and explains that management is difficult to demonstrate on benchmarks, with evidence arriving only after weeks or months.

r002.rationale: For large organizations, the candidate predicts adoption will involve managers increasingly delegating the mechanical parts of their jobs to AI.

astra-6.text:
I expect it to happen gradually, and probably unevenly across different kinds of management. You might first see an AI that’s very good at taking a project, breaking it down into tasks, assigning those tasks to other AI systems, and checking whether the results actually fit together. That’s a setting where you can test its capabilities fairly directly.

Managing people is a somewhat different problem. Even if an AI gives good advice about what a team should do, people have to trust it, and someone has to take responsibility when things go wrong. So I’d expect adoption there to start with managers using AI to help make decisions, with more authority delegated over time if that works well.

The strongest evidence would be organizations using these systems and consistently getting better results. You don’t need everyone to agree in advance that AI can manage. If some firms demonstrate that it works, others have an incentive to follow. But there could be a substantial gap between having the capability and figuring out how to reorganize an institution around it.

r001.rationale: The response describes a substantial gap between having management capability and reorganizing institutions around it, but does not clearly say recognition of the capability will lag its emergence.

r002.rationale: It predicts adoption will start with managers using AI to help make decisions, with more authority delegated over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect it to happen gradually, through people delegating increasingly complicated tasks. Initially, you might use an AI to do a fairly well-specified piece of work. But if it can break that work into subtasks, assign those subtasks to other AI systems, and check the results, then you’re already using something like management capability, even if you don’t call it that.

Recognition may lag behind capability, because management is harder to evaluate than an individual task. You need to see whether a system can deliver a project over time, handle unexpected problems, and make sensible tradeoffs. A convincing demonstration would be an AI taking responsibility for a project and completing it with relatively little human intervention.

Adoption will probably start where feedback is fast and mistakes are cheap. If those systems consistently deliver good results, people will give them more responsibility. I wouldn’t expect companies to immediately hand over an entire organization. I’d expect the scope of delegation to expand as people gain experience with what works.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says recognition may lag behind capability, because management is harder to evaluate than individual tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes gradual adoption through increasingly complex delegation, but does not say that managers will integrate AI into their own workflows.
